newsitem.title: UK: Mark profits from EMU, poll fears in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Mark profits from EMU, poll fears in late Europe.

text.p: The French franc sank to seven-week lows against the mark in late Europe, hauling down the lira with it, as a quiet market fretted over French opinion polls and the implications of the forthcoming French election for European monetary union.
An IPSOS survey for weekly Le Point released late Thursday predicted France's centre-right ruling coalition would scrape just a narrow majority in the May 25/June 1 parliamentary election.
The local elections to be held in Italy on Sunday did the lira no favours, sparking fears the Communists' hand would be strengthened and fiscal tightening jeopardised, analysts said.
The mark climbed to 3.3773/74 French francs and 997.20/60 by 1418 GMT from late Thursday's European levels of 3.3744/49 and 994.00/40.
Traders said market holidays in several European centres, including Italy, had dampened trading, as had a rangebound performance by the dollar ahead of this weekend's G7 meeting.
But simmering fears France's Socialists could take power and cast into question the country's EMU efforts dominated dealings.
"The lira...is more highly geared towards EMU sentiment in many ways than even the franc, so that's being hurt too," said Julius Baer Investments' international economist Adrian Owens.
A member of the Socialist party leadership sounded the hard line on EMU in French business daily La Tribune Desfosses.

Pierre Moscovici told the paper the Socialists, if elected, would insist Italy was included in the launch of the euro and would negotiate with other EU members to "refine the economic convergence criterion in trends (rather than fixed figures)".
This would mean "the decision to enter the euro will be taken on a political basis and not an accountancy basis", La Tribune quoted Moscovici as saying.
A Bundesbank council member also talked late yesterday of the political influences at play in the single currency process.
Helmut Hesse said EU political leaders had scope to allow a small overshoot of the Maastricht Treaty's criterion requiring budget deficits of no more than three percent of GDP.
"The deficit criterion will not be regarded as fulfilled or not fulfilled by looking at the statistics. It will be a political decision," Hesse told reporters.
His colleague Reimut Jochimsen said today EMU could only start on time with a small group of countries and that delay could not be "categorically ruled out".
Chancellor Helmut Kohl insisted, however, that Germany would never accept delay and would meet all the EMU criteria.
The market was also wary ahead of this weekend's Group of Seven meeting, amid fears the major industrial nations would attempt to curb the dollar's strength.
Dollar/yen is thought to be a greater bugbear for the authorities than dollar/mark, but the risk of a weakening U.S. unit was one more burden on the mark satellites, analysts said.

"For Italy and France the underlying background is beginning to deteriorate. If we saw a turnaround in the dollar, that would clearly compound the problems for the crosses," said Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas.
"We're on the verge perhaps of a much more volatile period for the foreign exchange markets."
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
